chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
title: Being identified with one song and keeping the repertoire current
summary: She says she was stuck with 'Loch Lomond' as an attraction but kept her repertoire fresh.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: Well you see, the only band that you'd say I was really affiliated with was the John Kirby Orchestra, that is over any length of time or established any particular kind of style. Because after that on the vaudeville road, I was with different bands, arrangements were, more or less, stock arrangements and I didn't get a chance to develop any particular singing style. It was just the type of songs that I did that stood out.

Well, I'm sure most people would not agree with you there. You haven't developed a singing style. Maybe people are paying attention to the wrong songs and not listening to the more representative selections from your recorded output.

when you get stuck with a song and you're considered an attraction, they really don't hear anything else except for what you're supposed to be noted for, and I've been billed as "The 'Loch Lomond' Lady" for so long. I sort of get a little up tight when I've sung my heart out on other songs and somebody says, when are you going to do "Loch Lomond"?

As far back as 1942 when I went into Le Ruban Bleu, I was being interviewed by one of the reporters from a local newspaper and he asked me if I was going to include "Loch Lomond" in my repertoire and I said I would hope not and the reporter said, 'So do we, so do we, so do we.' And that was as far back as 1942. And I think one of the things that really annowed me during my singing career was the fact that I was more or less stuck with "Loch Lomond" and by 1957 when I decided to give up, I mean, how many times can you do "Loch Lomond"? And that's one of the things that caused me to sort of drop out of the scene. Of course it's kind of crazy. I think of other singers, and of course now, with the revival of the interest in nostalgia, you know, any

of the singers if they appear someplace they're going to expect them to sing the songs they're identified with say, thirty or forty years ago. But it really annowed me. I was never received as a singer of anything else but "Loch Loman". Now, that is on a wide commercial sense. In the clubs where I appeared naturally I sang other songs. I was in Le Ruban Bleu on and off for six years and although "Loch Loman" was part of my repertoire, even the current tunes were changed, you know, you wouldn't be singing the same songs.

I kept pretty much up to date with my repertoire. And I have done alot of things that I had though I did a whole lot better than "Loch Loman". And right now I don't, one of the reasons why I don't do those things because they wouldn't sound like they did in the early days. I was younger and my voice was a little different. It's maturated now. It's a little deeper.
